solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Being careless connected pair likely to slip

indicators.note: something done carelessly is left in a mess, so the letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Two people tied together, one careless, are both liable to take a tumble, like roped climbers.
explanation.walkthrough: The thirteen letters of 'connected pair' rearrange to ACCIDENT-PRONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone accident-prone tends to have mishaps, so is the sort of person liable to trip or fall.

clue.text: See building here?

blocks.note: surface reading: an invitation to look at a construction on this spot
setter's reading: a see is a bishop's diocese, so this is the principal church of a diocese

explanation.surface: A guide points at a site and tells visitors to look at the building there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb but is the noun for a bishop's seat or diocese; the building at its heart is the CATHEDRAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral is the church containing the bishop's throne, the central building of his see or diocese.

clue.text: European country — one replacing established old region of Asia Minor

indicators.note: replacing says one item takes the place of another inside the named word

blocks.note: the Baltic state
Roman numeral for one
common abbreviation for established, as on shop signs

explanation.surface: A news item about one European nation being swapped for an established one.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the EST at the front of ESTONIA for I and you get IONIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionia was the ancient Greek coastal territory in western Anatolia, home to cities such as Ephesus and Miletus.

clue.text: Fat opera singers run at sight of short rodent

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the word for the creature loses its final letter

blocks.note: the English National Opera company
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run
a small rodent

explanation.surface: Plump opera singers flee in panic on spotting a little mouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The ENO is the English National Opera, London's opera company. The clue's 'Fat' has to stretch to mean very large.
explanation.definitionFit: Enormous means hugely big, and fat in the loose sense of large or substantial, as in a fat cheque.

clue.text: Slightly drunk artist prodding newlywed in the guts

indicators.note: the guts are the innards, so only the central letters of each word are kept

blocks.note: the central pair of a six-letter word
the central pair of an eight-letter word
the central pair of an eight-letter word

explanation.surface: A tipsy painter pokes a bridegroom in the stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the two middle letters of each of the three words in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiddly is informal British for a little intoxicated, merry rather than seriously inebriated.

clue.text: Criminal starts to read copy of a will

indicators.note: the starts are the opening letters, so only the beginning of the next word is used

blocks.note: the opening two letters
probate can mean the officially certified copy of a proved will

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer begins reading a copy of someone's will.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprobate is an unprincipled scoundrel, so a villain or lawbreaker in the loose sense of a bad lot.

clue.text: Present for Romans?

blocks.note: surface reading: a gift suitable for people of ancient Rome
setter's reading: the present time, an old word for it surviving in an idiom, dressed up with a Latin-looking ending

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what gift to give the ancient Romans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' is the time, not a gift: 'for the NONCE' means for the present. The question mark and 'Romans' hint at its Latin look, as NON and CE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonce means the present occasion, surviving almost only in the idiom 'for the nonce', meaning for now.

clue.text: Governing body reorganise NHS timetables

indicators.note: to reorganise is to put into a different order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: A health board orders a reshuffle of hospital schedules.
explanation.walkthrough: The NHS is Britain's National Health Service, which makes the surface sound like a management memo.
explanation.definitionFit: The Establishment is the ruling group that holds power and influence in a society, the authorities in charge.

clue.text: Meat hunter catching fresh Eel, Deer and Trotter?

indicators.note: fresh means new, so these letters are made into a new arrangement
a hunter catching something holds it inside, so one word surrounds the other

blocks.note: a whaler hunts whales, partly for their meat
the seven letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A butcher-hunter bags a fresh catch of eel, deer and pig's trotter.
explanation.walkthrough: Trotter is not a pig's foot but Del Boy Trotter, the market trader of the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses, the classic WHEELER-DEALER.
explanation.definitionFit: Del Boy Trotter is the archetypal shrewd, scheming trader, an example of a wheeler-dealer; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Fool sent back to court for occupying heavy tree

indicators.note: sent back means returned the other way, so the word is read from right to left
to occupy is to sit inside, so these letters go within the other word

blocks.note: sad can describe heavy, badly risen cake or bread
a nit is a fool, short for nitwit
to court is to woo

explanation.surface: A jester is returned to the royal court for living in a gloomy wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy' here is the baker's sense: a sad cake is one that failed to rise and stayed dense and sodden.
explanation.definitionFit: Satinwood is a tropical tree, notably of India and Sri Lanka, prized for its glossy timber.

clue.text: Dart back and check collar

indicators.note: back means going in the opposite direction, so the word is read right to left

blocks.note: to nip is to dart quickly somewhere
CH is the chess abbreviation for check

explanation.surface: A tailor nips back to inspect a shirt collar.
explanation.definitionFit: Collar and pinch are both slang for arrest, as when the police nab a suspect.

clue.text: After a kip return beer for pack-leader

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the drink is read backwards
after places the drink behind the earlier pieces in the line

blocks.note: taken as written
K is the abbreviation for the kip, the currency of Laos
ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: Someone back from a nap demands a beer to give the leader of the gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kip' looks like sleep, but it is the Laotian currency, abbreviated K.
explanation.definitionFit: Akela is the title of the adult leader of a Cub Scout pack, taken from the wolf in Kipling's Jungle Book.

clue.text: Before end of conference politician takes in the Spanish horror movie and Muse

indicators.note: to take in is to admit inside, so the politician surrounds the Spanish word
the end of a word is its last letter, so only that is kept
before means coming earlier in the line, so the preceding pieces go in front

blocks.note: Member of Parliament
el is Spanish for the
The Omen, the 1976 horror film
its final letter

explanation.surface: An MP at a conference fits in a Spanish horror film before the closing session, and finds inspiration.
explanation.definitionFit: Melpomene was one of the nine Muses of Greek myth, the one who presided over tragedy.

clue.text: Plant's shoot behind bird

indicators.note: behind means coming after, so the shoot follows the bird in the line

blocks.note: a songbird
a spur is a short side shoot on a plant

explanation.surface: A gardener notes a plant's new shoot just behind where a bird is perched.
explanation.definitionFit: Larkspur is a flowering garden plant, a delphinium relative with tall spikes of blue flowers.

clue.text: Lush large visor, as it were

blocks.note: a lush is a drunkard, as is a sot
OS stands for outsize, a clothing size
the peak of a cap is its visor

explanation.surface: A rich, oversized visor, or something like one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush' looks like an adjective for luxuriant, but it is the noun for a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: So to speak and as it were are both phrases admitting that what was said is figurative or loosely put.

clue.text: Little girl's fib about donkey

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for a fib goes around the animal

blocks.note: a fib is a lie
an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: A small girl tells a white lie about her pet donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: LASSIE is Scottish and northern English for a young girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassie is a diminutive of lass, a girl, so it names a young or little girl.

clue.text: Type of painting not influenced by any movement?

definitions.text: Type of painting not influenced by any movement?

blocks.note: surface reading: an independent painting style owing nothing to any artistic school
setter's reading: a picture of objects that are motionless, with nothing in it moving

explanation.surface: A critic describes a style of painting that owes nothing to any art movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement' suggests an art school like Cubism; read literally it means motion, and a STILL LIFE depicts motionless objects.
explanation.definitionFit: A still life is a genre of painting depicting inanimate objects such as fruit, flowers or vessels.

clue.text: Curly kale I put in before lots of water

indicators.note: curly suggests twisted round, so the leafy vegetable's letters are bent into another order
to put something in is to place it inside, so the letter goes within the next word

blocks.note: its four letters rearranged
ere is an old word for before
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe: put curly kale into a dish ahead of plenty of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Erie is one of the North American Great Lakes, a huge body of fresh water.

clue.text: Greet large cook outside

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so the cooking word wraps around the size letter

blocks.note: to sauté is to fry quickly
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A host welcomes a big chef standing out of doors.
explanation.definitionFit: To salute someone is to acknowledge or hail them with a formal gesture, so to greet them.

clue.text: Nervously admire extremely big pheasant

indicators.note: something done nervously is jittery and unsettled, so these letters get jumbled
the extremes of a word are its ends, so only its first and last letters are used

blocks.note: taken as written
its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone timidly admires a very large pheasant.
explanation.definitionFit: The pheasant is an example of a game bird, a wild bird shot for sport and food; the definition names one case.

clue.text: Racehorse trainer put pressure on Italian staff

indicators.note: to put one thing on another is to stack them, so the pieces are placed one after the other

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
common abbreviation for Italian
to man is to staff, as in man the desk

explanation.surface: A horse trainer leans on Italian stable staff.
explanation.walkthrough: Jenny Pitman is a famous British racehorse trainer, the first woman to train a Grand National winner.
explanation.definitionFit: Jenny Pitman trained National Hunt racehorses in Britain, so she is an example of a racehorse trainer.

clue.text: Drunk homes in on hooch

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so these letters reel into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker zeroes in on the bootleg liquor.
explanation.definitionFit: Moonshine is illicitly distilled spirit, and hooch is slang for that same crude liquor.

clue.text: Head off for seller of tights — it's Twiggy!

indicators.note: taking the head off removes the top, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a hosier sells stockings and socks

explanation.surface: A hosiery shop recruits a famously thin model to sell its tights.
explanation.walkthrough: Twiggy was a famous 1960s British model; here the word just means made of twigs, as the OSIER willow is used for wickerwork.
explanation.definitionFit: An osier is a willow whose long pliant shoots or twigs are used in basketry, so it is twiggy indeed.

clue.text: A hunk carried back wood

indicators.note: carried back means taken the opposite way, so the phrase is read right to left

blocks.note: a slab is a thick hunk, with A as written

explanation.surface: Someone lugs a big chunk back to the timber yard.
explanation.definitionFit: Balsa is a very light timber from a tropical American tree, used for models and rafts.

clue.text: Old couch providing support for Bishop and former leader

indicators.note: in a down clue support sits underneath, so this piece goes below the other

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
lair once meant a bed or resting place

explanation.surface: An antique sofa props up a bishop and an ex-prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was British Prime Minister from 1997 to 2007. Lair's old sense of a couch or bed survives in an animal's den.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony Blair was formerly leader of the Labour Party and of the UK government, so a past leader.

clue.text: Hooter I carried making this?

indicators.note: something carried is held within, so the word for a hooter holds the letter

blocks.note: hooter is slang for nose
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone carrying a car horn asks whether they are the one making the racket.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a hooter, whether horn or nose, makes a din.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooter is a horn or siren, and the sound it makes is a loud din, the sort of row the answer names.

clue.text: Soldier at sea eats fish spread

indicators.note: to eat something is to take it inside, so the soldier surrounds the fish

blocks.note: a marine is a soldier serving on ships
a gar is a long-snouted fish

explanation.surface: A sailor-soldier tucks into a fish paste.
explanation.definitionFit: Margarine is a butter substitute spread on bread, so a spread in the table sense.

clue.text: Hear Ted is distraught!

blocks.note: surface reading: a cry that someone called Ted is upset
setter's reading: these two words are a broken-up, rearranged form of the second half of the answer, so they describe it

explanation.surface: Someone urges listeners to hear poor Ted, who is in a terrible state.
explanation.walkthrough: This is reverse wordplay: HEARTED, broken, gives HEAR TED, so the answer's own words BROKEN HEARTED are the instruction that produces the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone brokenhearted is overwhelmed with grief or sorrow, so as upset as a distraught person.
